etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English charme, from Old French charme (“chant, magic spell”), from Latin carmen (“song, incantation”).

definitions.definition: An object, act or words believed to have magic power (usually carries a positive connotation).
(often in the plural) The ability to persuade, delight or arouse admiration.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VIII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: […] the charm of Beauties powerful glance.

quote.citation: 1697, [William] Congreve, The Mourning Bride, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act I, page 1:
quote.text: Muſick has Charms to ſooth a ſavage Breaſt,  To ſoften Rocks, or bend a knotted Oak.

quote.citation: 1714, Alexander Pope, “The Rape of the Lock”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], published 1717, →OCLC, canto V, page 160:
quote.text: Charms ſtrike the ſight, but merit wins the ſoul.

quote.citation: 1769, Firishta, translated by Alexander Dow, Tales translated from the Persian of Inatulla of Delhi, volume I, Dublin: P. and W. Wilson et al., page 15:
quote.text: Her coyneſs was conquered by aſſiduity, and at laſt ſhe conſented to reſign the treaſure of her charms to my paſſion.

definitions.definition: A small trinket on a bracelet or chain, etc., traditionally supposed to confer luck upon the wearer.
The collective noun for a group of goldfinches.
(particle physics) A quantum number of hadrons determined by the number of charm quarks and antiquarks.

quote.citation: 1975 July 31, Sandra Blakeslee, “Another Particle Believed Discovered”, in The New York Times‎[1], →ISSN:
quote.text: In trying to understand the long life of the psi particle, physicists postulated the notion of “charm.” Charm, they say, prevents the “easy” decay of particles and thus prolongs their lifetimes. U particles, Dr. Pert said, may carry the property of charm.

quote.citation: 2020, James E. Dodd, Ben Gripaios, The Ideas of Particle Physics, Cambridge University Press, →ISBN, page 173:
quote.text: Mesons which combine the charmed quark with the up or down antiquarks are  denoted the D mesons. These mesons carry explicit charm (i.e. have a non-zero  charm quantum number), just as the K mesons carry strangeness.

definitions.definition: (finance) A second-order measure of derivative price sensitivity, expressed as the instantaneous rate of change of delta with respect to time.
(graphical user interface, Microsoft Windows) An icon providing quick access to a command or setting.

quote.text: Undoubtedly one of the most important pieces to navigating Windows 8, charms are actually not visible until a command to show them is given.

definitions.definition: To seduce, persuade or fascinate someone or something.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: […] they, on thir mirth & dance / Intent, with jocond Muſic charm his ear;

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC, page 58:
quote.text: The Celebrity, by arts unknown, induced Mrs. Judge Short and two other ladies to call at Mohair on a certain afternoon when Mr. Cooke was trying a trotter on the track. The three returned wondering and charmed with Mrs. Cooke; they were sure she had had no hand in the furnishing of that atrocious house.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To use a magical charm upon; to subdue, control, or summon by incantation or supernatural influence; to ensorcel or exert a magical effect on.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii], page 389, column 2:

definitions.definition: To protect with, or make invulnerable by, spells, charms, or supernatural influences.

quote.citation: 1611 April (first recorded performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Cymbeline”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii], page 393, column 1:
quote.text: I, in mine owne woe charm’d, / Could not finde death, […]

quote.citation: 1579, Immeritô [pseudonym; Edmund Spenser], “October. Ægloga Decima.”, in The Shepheardes Calender: […], London:  […]  Hugh Singleton, […], →OCLC, folio 42, recto:
quote.text: But ah my corage cooles ere it be warme, / For thy, content vs in thys humble ſhade: / Where no ſuch troublous tydes han vs aſſayde, / Here we our ſlender pipes may ſafely charme.

definitions.definition: To subdue or overcome by some secret power, or by that which gives pleasure; to allay; to soothe.

quote.citation: 1687 (date written), Alexander Pope, “Ode for Musick on St. Cecilia’s Day”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], →OCLC, canto VII, page 378:
quote.text: Music the fierceſt griefs can charm, / And fate's ſevereſt rage diſarm:  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Variant of chirm, from Middle English chirme, from Old English ċierm (“cry, alarm”), from Proto-Germanic *karmiz.

definitions.definition: The mixed sound of many voices, especially of birds or children.

quote.citation: 1591, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “The Teares of the Muses”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. […], London:  […]  William Ponsonbie, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: […] Free libertie to chaunt our charmes at will: […]

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book IV”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Sweet is the breath of morn, her riſing ſweet,  With charm of earlieſt Birds;

quote.citation: 1955, William Golding, The Inheritors, Faber and Faber, published 2005, page 152:
quote.text: The laughter rose like the charm of starlings.

quote.citation: 2018, Holly Ringland, The Lost Flowers of Alice Hart:
quote.text: A charm of finches flew overhead, singing into the vivid afternoon sky.
